title: DTRU: A Versatile, Compact, Simple, and Robust NTRU KEM with Double $E_8$ Encoding
authors: Hengchuan Zou, Songlin Li, Jieyu Zheng, Xiaowen Hu, Hanyu Wei, Weizhi Ao, Yifan Dong, Wenbo Guo, and Yunlei Zhao
abstract:
Responding to China's 2025 call for commercial cryptographic standards mandating 128-bit, 256-bit, and 512-bit security (optional 384-bit), we propose DTRU, a versatile, compact, simple, and robust NTRU-based key encapsulation mechanism (KEM). Our principal design contribution is double $E_8$ encoding, which constructs 16-dimensional lattice codes from $E_8$ with low decoding complexity. We further provide a detailed analysis of decryption-failure probability under this encoding mechanism. 

DTRU's design achieves a careful balance among versatility, compactness, simplicity, and robustness. To accommodate diverse application requirements, it supports multiple ring structures, including power-of-two cyclotomic rings, tricyclotomic rings, and large-Galois-group prime-degree prime-ideal number fields (LPPNF). The double $E_8$ encoding enables DTRU to achieve enhanced error correction with compact bandwidth. The design prioritizes simplicity to facilitate deployment on low-power devices, achieved by eschewing additional coefficient compression techniques and redundant invertibility checks during key generation, while enabling circuit/code reuse. Security robustness is guaranteed through parameter selections that offer adequate security redundancy, mitigating potential cyclotomic ring risks via LPPNF, and precluding sparse noise distributions in the recommended parameter sets.

Complementing our theoretical advances, we present comprehensive implementations of all the parameter sets with dedicated support for C, AVX2, and ARM platforms, leveraging architecture-specific optimizations. For example, compared to NTRU-HRSS and Kyber at the same security levels, our KEM is 49%-52% more compact and 3.84–15.69$\times$ faster than NTRU-HRSS in the round-trip time of ephemeral key exchange, and is 7%-27% more compact and 1.05–1.32$\times$ faster than Kyber.

1     Introduction

Shor’s quantum algorithm [35] can efficiently solve problems such as integer fac-
torization, undermining the security of many widely used public-key schemes
2        H. Zou et al.

and motivating the development of post-quantum cryptography (PQC). One
prominent direction within PQC is based on NTRU lattices. NTRU [23], first
proposed in 1998, has played a foundational role in many modern cryptographic
constructions [13,17,19,14,6,28]. Contemporary NTRU-style schemes are typi-
cally justified under two hardness assumptions: the decisional NTRU assumption
and the Ring-LWE assumption (some variants instead rely on the Ring-LWR as-
sumption). During the NIST PQC standardization process NTRU reached the
third round as a finalist but was not selected; a main reason was that it was
neither the fastest nor the most compact among the lattice-based KEM finalists.
Consequently, much subsequent work has concentrated on improving NTRU’s
efficiency and reducing its bandwidth.
     The original NTRU’s ring choice Zq [x]/(xn − 1) with prime n is incompatible
with the Number Theoretic Transform (NTT). Although alternative multiplica-
tion strategies (e.g., NTT-unfriendly methods [10] or Toom-Cook [3]) are avail-
able, they incur performance overheads. Moving to NTT-friendly rings is there-
fore a natural optimization to achieve substantial speedups, as in NTTRU [31]
and NTRU+ [26]. Another line of work, exemplified by BAT [18], focuses on
ciphertext compression by adopting the Ring-LWR assumption and exploiting
NTRU structure for faster integer arithmetic, albeit at the cost of increased
key-generation complexity.
     Recent approaches like NEV [37] and DAWN [30] seek to optimize the
bandwidth-performance tradeoff. NEV employs vector encoding that maps plain-
text bits to multiple coefficient MSBs (similar to repetition coding), enhancing
decryption robustness. Its variant NEV′ , while improving noise tolerance, relies
on the non-standard sspRLWE assumption. DAWN utilizes zero-divisor encod-
ing for stronger ciphertext compression with negligible decryption failure, and
introduces a double-encoding paradigm. However, DAWN requires an additional
polynomial inversion and employs sparse noise. Both schemes are confined to
power-of-two cyclotomic rings Zq [x]/(xn + 1), restricting ring and parameter
choices.


1.1    Our Contributions

In October 2025, the Institute of Commercial Cryptography Standards of China
issued a call for commercial cryptographic algorithm standards, mandating sup-
port for at least three classical security strength levels: 128-bits, 256-bits, and
512-bits, with optional 384-bits support1 . In response to this requirement, we
present DTRU, a versatile, compact, simple, and robust NTRU-based key encap-
sulation mechanism that achieves provable IND-CCA security under the NTRU
and Ring-LWE assumptions.

Versatility through Multiple Instantiations DTRU supports multiple mathemat-
ical instantiations to accommodate diverse security and performance require-
ments. Our primary instantiation utilizes tricyclotomic rings (Zq [x]/(xn −xn/2 +

1), following the approach in [31]), which enables seamless support for classical
security levels spanning 128, 192, 256, 384, and 512 bits. For enhanced secu-
rity assurance, we introduce DTRU-Prime, which operates on large-Galois-group
prime-degree prime-ideal number fields (LPPNF, specifically Zq [x]/(xn − x − 1))
to provide conservative defense against potential algebraic attacks through
subring- and subfield-free structures. Additionally, we present DTRU-Light, a
lightweight variant based on power-of-two cyclotomic rings (Zq [x]/(xn + 1)) op-
timized for resource-constrained devices. This multi-faceted instantiation capa-
bility underscores the exceptional versatility of the DTRU framework.

Compactness via Advanced Encoding and Simple Design We employ double E8
encoding to enhance error correction capabilities, achieving remarkable com-
pactness. The design prioritizes simplicity to facilitate deployment on low-power
devices, achieved by eschewing additional coefficient compression techniques and
redundant invertibility checks during key generation, while enabling circuit/code
reuse.

Robust Security Design DTRU’s robust security design incorporates adequate
parameter security redundancy, LPPNF instantiation (Zq [x]/(xn − x − 1) as
in [7]) with subring- and subfield-free structures to defend against algebraic
attacks, and the exclusion of sparse noise distributions through centered binomial
distributions (parameter at least 2 for most configurations). These measures
collectively enhance DTRU’s security robustness.

Technical Innovation: Double E8 Encoding Our key technical contribution is a
novel lattice-encoding technique, double E8 encoding, which synergistically com-
bines NEV’s repetition encoding with an extended Hamming-style code derived
from the E8 lattice. This approach achieves superior error correction by mapping
4 bits to 16 coefficients, resulting in a significantly enhanced minimum Euclidean
distance that dramatically reduces decryption failure rates while maintaining ef-
ficient decoding performance.

Practical Efficiency and Performance Validation Our comprehensive implemen-
tation and benchmarking demonstrate DTRU’s practical efficiency. In C im-
plementations, DTRU achieves 8.76-15.69× speedup over traditional NTRU
schemes and 1.05-1.32× improvement over Kyber. With AVX2 optimizations,
DTRU maintains 3.84-6.28× performance gains over NTRU schemes while de-
livering 1.10-1.22× improvement over Kyber. On ARM Cortex-M4 embedded
systems, DTRU consistently outperforms Kyber with 1.06-1.62× speedup. These
results validate the practical efficiency of our double E8 encoding approach across
diverse computing platforms.

    Benchmarking on x86 and ARM platforms shows our KEM achieves 3.84-

Definition 1 (Public-Key Encryption). A public key encryption scheme
(PKE) over message space M is a tuple of algorithms (gen, enc, dec) defined
as follows:
(1) (pk, sk) ← gen(1κ ): The key generation algorithm gen takes as input the se-
curity parameter and outputs a key pair (pk, sk). For brevity, the input to gen is

Definition 3 (Key Encapsulation Mechanism). A key encapsulation mech-
anism (KEM) over key space K is a tuple of algorithms (Gen, Encaps, Decaps)
defined as follows:
(1) (pk, sk) ← Gen(1κ ): The key generation algorithm Gen takes as input the
security parameter and outputs a key pair (pk, sk). For brevity, the input to Gen
is often omitted.
(2) (ct, K) ← Encaps(pk): The encapsulation algorithm takes as input the public
key pk and outputs a tuple (ct, K), where K ∈ K and ct ∈ C.
(3) K ′ ← Decaps(sk, ct): The decapsulation algorithm, given the secret key sk
and ciphertext ct, outputs a key K ′ . If the KEM supports explicit rejection, the
output is K ′ ∈ K or the rejection symbol ⊥.

3     Double E8 Encoding for NTRU-based KEMs
In this section, we present the double E8 encoding scheme that underlies the
DTRU construction. We begin by reviewing the NEV approach, then describe
how we enhance the encoding with lattice coding derived from the E8 lattice to
achieve stronger error correction.

3.2   Double E8 Encoding
Our construction, DTRU, aims to encode n/4 bits into n coefficients. This encod-
ing requirement necessitates a binary code that maps 1 bit to 2 bits on average.
When combined with NEV’s repetition code, this yields a 1-to-4 mapping.
    Building upon this foundation, we further enhance error correction by in-
creasing the encoding dimension. Specifically, we employ a four-dimensional sub-
lattice of the E8 lattice to construct an extended Hamming-style code that maps
4 bits to 8 bits, achieving a minimum Hamming distance of 4, an optimal prop-
erty among binary [8,4] codes. The combination of this extended Hamming-style
code with NEV’s repetition encoding yields a double E8 encoding that effectively
maps 4 bits to 16 coordinates while maintaining modest decoding complexity.

Message Encoding The core component of our double E8 encoding is the E8
code, which is constructed from a four-dimensional sublattice of the E8 lattice.
To encode a message m ∈ {0, 1}4 , we compute the codeword u = mH mod 2,
where H is the generator matrix defined as follows:

4     NTRU Encryption Scheme with Double E8 Encoding
In this section, we present our NTRU encryption scheme with double E8 encod-
ing, referred to as DTRU.PKE, as well as its corresponding key encapsulation
mechanism, DTRU.KEM. Furthermore, we analyze the error rate of the scheme
and establish its provable security under standard cryptographic assumptions.

4.1   Algorithms of DTRU.PKE with Double E8 encoding
The algorithms for key generation, encryption, and decryption in our DTRU
public key encryption scheme are formally presented in Fig. 2.
    The DTRU.PKE scheme follows a standard NTRU-based encryption frame-
work with several key innovations. The algorithm flow consists of three main
components:
    Key Generation: The scheme generates a key pair (pk, sk) = (h, f ), where
f = pf ′ + 1 is constructed to ensure invertibility in the ring Rq . The parameter p
is chosen based on the ring structure: p = 2 for tricyclotomic rings and LPPNF,
or p = 1 − xn/2 for power-of-two cyclotomic rings. This parameter selection is
specifically designed to minimize the error rate, as analyzed in the subsequent
error rate analysis.
    Encryption: The encryption process samples noise polynomials r and e,
encodes the message m using double E8 encoding, and computes the cipher-
text. A key feature is the compression operation ⌊ qq2 (·)⌉ mod q2 , which reduces
ciphertext size by compressing from modulus q to q2 .
    Decryption: Decryption reverses the compression to recover the original
modulus, then uses the secret key f to recover the encoded message, which is
decoded back to the plaintext.

5     Concrete Security and Parameter Selection
This section analyzes the security of the DTRU scheme, which relies on the com-
putational hardness of RLWE and NTRU problems. We evaluate their resilience
against state-of-the-art cryptanalytic techniques.

5.1   Concrete Attacks on RLWE
To evaluate the security strength of the RLWE problem, we adopt the Core-SVP
framework and analyze various attack methodologies.
    Since standard lattice reduction algorithms like BKZ cannot directly exploit
the algebraic structure of RLWE, except for certain weak instances identified
in [8,16], we first transform the RLWE instance into an equivalent LWE instance
for analysis.
    Given an RLWE instance (a, t = as + e) ∈ Rq × Rq , we transform it to an
LWE instance as follows: Let a ∈ Znq be the coefficient vector of polynomial a,
and define the matrix A ∈ Zn×n  q   as the matrix representation of multiplication
by a in the ring Rq . Similarly, let s, e, t ∈ Znq be the coefficient vectors of s, e, t
respectively. Then the RLWE instance becomes the LWE instance:

                           (A, t = As + e) ∈ Zn×n
                                              q   × Znq .

Core-SVP Methodology. BKZ-class attacks [9] represent the most effective
methods against RLWE. These attacks transform the LWE problem into a short
vector problem (SVP) on a lattice using embedding techniques (Kannan embed-
ding [24] and Bai-Galbraith embedding [5]), then solve the SVP using the BKZ
lattice basis reduction algorithm.
            DTRU: A Versatile, Compact, Simple, and Robust NTRU KEM             15

    The BKZ algorithm iteratively examines b-dimensional projected sublattices,
solving the SVP on these sublattices using enumeration or sieving. The reduced
basis vectors follow the geometric series assumption, enabling estimation of the
block size b required to solve the SVP, which provides the security estimate. For
our security assessment, we utilize the modern cost framework presented in [32].
Primal Attack. The primal attack reduces LWE to solving the unique shortest
vector problem (u-SVP). Given (A, t = As + e), we construct an (n + m + 1)-
dimensional lattice:

           L = x ∈ Zn+m+1 | (A[1:m] | Im | −t[1:m] )x ≡ 0 (mod q)
                 

where m ≤ n. The lattice basis matrix is:

The unique p shortest vector v = (sT | eT | 1)T in L solves the LWE problem,
with ∥v∥ ≈ α12 n + α22 m.
Dual Attack. The dual attack finds short vectors in the dual lattice. Given
(A, t), we construct the dual lattice:

               L∗ = (x, y) ∈ Zm × Zn | AT[1:m] x = y (mod q)

A short vector (x, y) ∈ L∗ allows recovery of s[m+1:n] through:

               ⟨x, t⟩ = ⟨x, e⟩ + ⟨y, s[1:m] ⟩ + ⟨AT[m+1:n] x, s[m+1:n] ⟩.

BKW attack. The Blum-Kalai-Wasserman (BKW) algorithm employs com-
binatorial techniques rather than lattice reduction. Recent composite ap-
proaches [21,27] have enhanced BKW’s efficiency, making it the most effective
attack for specific parameter regimes.
Algebraic attack. Algebraic attacks, introduced in [4], construct equations for
the variables s[1:m] from the small set e[1:m] , yielding n high-degree equations
in n variables. These are typically solved using Gröbner basis computations. In
practice, however, algebraic approaches often provide limited advantage.

5.2   Concrete Attacks on NTRU
Similar to the RLWE instance, the NTRU instance (h = f −1 g mod q) ∈ Rq
can be viewed as a RLWE instance (h, 0 = hf − g) ∈ Rq × Rq with a zero
target vector, which can be transformed into the corresponding LWE instances
(H ′ , 0 = H ′ f − g) ∈ Zn×n
                         q   × Znq for analysis.
    While most attack methods on RLWE can be applied to NTRU, the dual
attack [1] is not applicable. The dual attack relies on a non-zero target vector
t′ to recover the secret through the computation ⟨x, t′ ⟩ = ⟨x, e⟩ + ⟨y, s⟩. In the
NTRU-to-LWE transformation, the target vector becomes zero, rendering this
mechanism ineffective.

Appendix A              Benchmarks and Comparisons
We benchmark our schemes and related works on a 64-bit Ubuntu Linux system
with an Intel i9-14900K CPU and 64 GB memory, reporting average CPU cycles
over 100000 runs in Table 3. All implementations use identical optimization flags
                DTRU: A Versatile, Compact, Simple, and Robust NTRU KEM                             19

“-march=native -mtune=native -O3 -fomit-frame-pointer”. The table groups re-
sults by security levels, where “Speedup” denotes the ratio of total Ref/AVX2
cycles for ephemeral key exchange relative to the first scheme in each group. We
did not include DAWN and NEV because they are not open source. Compared
to the similarly structured NTRU lattice-based constructions NTRU-HPS and
NTRU-HRSS, the Ref implementation shows an improvement of 8.76 to 15.69
times, while the AVX2 implementation achieves an enhancement of 3.84 to 6.28
times. Additionally, when compared to SNTRU-Prime, the DTRU-Prime Ref
implementation improves performance by 30.85 times. Compared to Kyber, our
solution achieves a performance improvement of 1.05 to 1.32 times in the Ref
implementation, and 1.10 to 1.22 times in the AVX2 implementation. Therefore,
compared to alternatives with the same security level, our scheme demonstrates
superior performance.
